why.es: Respuesta indirecta a un lamento: el concierto se anunció toda la semana, así que podría haberse enterado. C trata el concierto como algo futuro, pero ya ocurrió; B repite "concert" y "know".

screen.title: Academic Talk: Why wider roads fill up

audio.text: Today I want to look at a puzzle that city planners have struggled with for decades. When a highway is crowded, the obvious solution seems to be adding more lanes. More space for cars should mean less traffic, right? Yet study after study has found that within a few years, the widened road is often just as crowded as before.

Planners call this induced demand. When driving becomes faster and easier, people change their behavior. Someone who used to take the train starts driving instead. Someone who avoided rush hour starts leaving at eight rather than seven. Some families even move farther out, because the commute now seems manageable. All these small decisions add up to more cars, until traffic is back where it started. Some studies have even found that traffic grows almost exactly in step with the amount of new road space.

Now, this doesn't mean new roads are never useful. A road linking two towns that had no direct connection can make a real difference. screen.title: Academic Talk: When children say "goed"
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in a linguistics class.

audio.text: Here's something parents often notice. A two-year-old correctly says "I went" or "two feet." Then, a few months later, the same child starts saying "I goed" and "two foots." It looks as if the child's language is getting worse. In fact, it's a sign of progress. Let me explain why.

Linguists call these errors overregularization. At first, children seem to learn each past-tense form as a separate word, simply by copying what they hear. "Went" is just another word. But as their vocabulary grows, they begin to notice a pattern: most English verbs form the past by adding "-ed." Once they've worked out that rule, they apply it everywhere, even to irregular verbs they used to get right. The same thing happens with plurals, which is where "foots" comes from.

The key point is that children almost never hear forms like "goed" from adults. So they can't be imitating. They're producing something new from a rule they've discovered on their own. Eventually, with enough exposure, the correct irregular forms come back, and the rule is used only where it belongs. Researchers call this U-shaped development: performance starts high, drops, and then recovers, and the dip in the middle actually reflects deeper learning.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Cooling buildings with wind catchers
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an architecture class.

audio.text: Long before air conditioning, builders in hot, dry regions found ways to keep interiors comfortable. One of the most elegant is the wind catcher, a tall tower rising above the roof, which you can still see in parts of Iran and around the Persian Gulf. Near the top, the tower has openings that face the prevailing wind.

The basic principle is simple. Wind enters the openings and is pushed down a shaft into the rooms below, while warm indoor air escapes through windows or another part of the tower. Moving air feels cooler on the skin, even when its temperature doesn't change. But many wind catchers went further. Some sent the incoming air over a pool of water or through an underground channel before it reached the living spaces. As the water evaporated, it absorbed heat, so the air arriving inside really was several degrees cooler.

Interestingly, wind catchers can work even on still days. The tower's walls soak up sunlight, so the air inside the shaft warms up and rises, pulling fresh air through the house behind it. In other words, the tower acts as both a scoop and a chimney. Today, some architects are returning to the design, since it cools buildings without using any electricity.

audio.text: Today let's look at how bats find their way in complete darkness. Most bats rely on a process called echolocation. screen.title: Academic Talk: The rise of linear perspective
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an art history class.

audio.text: Let's turn to one of the great technical advances of the Renaissance: linear perspective. Before the fifteenth century, European painters certainly suggested depth. They placed distant figures higher in the picture or made them smaller, but they lacked a consistent system, and different objects in the same painting often seemed to recede at different angles.

In Florence, early in the fifteenth century, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small panel showing the city's baptistery and drilled a hole through it. A viewer looked through the hole from the back while holding a mirror in front of the panel, so the reflected painting could be compared directly with the real building. The two lined up remarkably well.

The principle behind this is that parallel lines moving away from the viewer appear to meet at a single point, which we now call the vanishing point. In the 1430s, Leon Battista Alberti described the method in writing, which allowed it to spread far beyond Brunelleschi's circle. Keep in mind, though, that perspective wasn't only about accuracy. Painters used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye, often toward the most important figure in the scene.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Path dependence
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: Let's talk about a concept economists call path dependence. The basic idea is that decisions made in the past can limit the choices available today, even when the original reasons no longer apply.

The classic example is the keyboard layout most of you are using right now, known as QWERTY. It was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. One popular explanation is that it placed common letter pairs apart so the metal arms wouldn't jam, although historians still argue about how much that really mattered. Either way, the jamming problem disappeared long ago. Other layouts have been designed since then. The Dvorak keyboard, for example, put the most common letters on the middle row, where your fingers already rest, and some people claim it's faster. Yet QWERTY is everywhere.

Why? Because once millions of people had learned it, and schools taught it, and manufacturers produced it, switching became very costly. A new layout would have to be better by enough to make everyone relearn typing at the same time. So the old standard survives, not necessarily because it's the best, but because everyone else is already using it. And economists find the same pattern whenever the value of a choice depends on what everyone else has already chosen.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Managing shared resources
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: In economics there's a well-known idea called the tragedy of the commons. Picture a pasture that everyone in a village may use. Each herder reasons that adding one more cow brings him the full benefit of that cow, while the cost, slightly less grass, is shared by everyone. So each herder adds cows, and eventually the pasture is ruined, even though no one wanted that outcome.

For a long time, economists assumed there were only two solutions: either the government controls the resource, or it's divided into private property. But the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged that view. She studied fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems around the world that communities had managed successfully for centuries without either solution.

What did those communities have in common? Ostrom found that they set clear boundaries around who could use the resource, they made their own rules about how much each person could take, and, this is important, they monitored one another and applied gradually increasing penalties to people who broke the rules. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this work. So the lesson isn't that shared resources are always doomed. It's that the outcome depends on how the users organize themselves.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The serial position effect
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

audio.text: Today I want to talk about something you've probably experienced without realizing it. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words and then ask you to write down as many as you can remember. Most people recall the first few words and the last few words quite well, but the words in the middle tend to disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

So why does it happen? The words at the beginning get more rehearsal. When you hear the first word, you repeat it to yourself a few times, and that repetition helps move it into long-term memory. By the time the middle of the list arrives, you're trying to rehearse many words at once, so each one gets less attention. The words at the end are a different story. They're still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can simply read them off, so to speak.

Here's the interesting part. If I make you wait thirty seconds and count backward before you write, the advantage for the final words disappears, but the advantage for the first words remains. That tells us two different memory systems are involved. So, practically speaking, when you study, try not to always start from the same page. Otherwise the middle chapters will always get the least attention.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The wolves of Yellowstone
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an environmental science class.

audio.text: In 1995, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park after an absence of about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology. Without wolves, elk had grazed freely along the rivers, eating young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Once wolves returned, the story goes, elk began avoiding open river valleys where they could easily be hunted. The trees recovered, beavers returned to use the wood, and their dams created ponds that supported fish and birds. Ecologists call a chain of effects like this a trophic cascade.

Now, it's a great story, and parts of it are clearly true. But more recent research suggests the picture is messier. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting by people, harsh winters, and a growing population of bears. And in some areas the willows haven't recovered at all, because without beaver dams the water table had dropped too low for the trees to grow back. In other words, removing a predator can trigger changes that simply adding it back doesn't reverse.
So what's the lesson? Not that the wolves didn't matter. They did. The lesson is that ecosystems don't always work like a light switch. Restoring one species is often only the first step.

text: Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?

Experimental evidence suggests a modest but measurable influence. In one study, Russian speakers distinguished between two shades of blue more rapidly when the shades straddled the boundary between goluboy and siniy than when both fell within a single category; English speakers showed no comparable advantage. Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.

Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

screen.title: Underground Fungal Networks
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Beneath most forests lies an extensive web of fungal threads known as mycorrhizal networks. These fungi colonize the roots of trees, supplying them with water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus in exchange for sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis.

Because a single network can connect the roots of many different trees, researchers have proposed that carbon and other resources may travel from one tree to another through these shared connections. Some experiments have reported that seedlings growing in deep shade receive carbon from larger neighbors, which might improve their chances of survival.

Nevertheless, the more dramatic claims, for instance that mature trees deliberately nurture their offspring or warn neighbors of insect attacks, remain contested. Critics note that many field studies were small, that the direction of transfer is difficult to measure, and that fungi may move resources primarily for their own benefit rather than for that of the forest.

why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis): las redes, lo que podrían hacer y las dudas sobre las afirmaciones más fuertes. C trata una afirmación discutida como un hecho.

screen.title: The Invention of Standard Time
text: Until the late nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, so the time in one city could differ by several minutes from the time in a city a short distance to the east or west.

This local system caused few problems while travel was slow. The arrival of railroads, however, changed the situation. Each railway company kept its own schedule, and a single station might display several clocks showing different times. Passengers often missed connections.

In 1883, railroads in the United States and Canada adopted a system of time zones, each differing from its neighbor by exactly one hour. Many communities at first resisted giving up "sun time," but the convenience of the new system gradually won acceptance.

screen.title: Urban Heat Islands
text: On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island. The main cause is the material that cities are built from: asphalt, concrete and brick absorb sunlight during the day and slowly release that heat at night.

Cities also lack the natural cooling that plants provide. Trees shade the ground, and they release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweat cools skin. Where green spaces are replaced by roads and buildings, this effect disappears.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. Warmer nights prevent people from recovering from daytime heat, and heat waves in cities are linked to more hospital visits. Some cities now paint roofs white, plant trees along streets and build parks, and early results suggest that these simple changes can lower local temperatures noticeably.

screen.title: Why Crickets Chirp

Crickets chirp faster when the air is warm and more slowly when it is cool, so some people use them to estimate the temperature.

screen.title: The First Coins
text: For thousands of years, people traded using pieces of metal, such as silver, whose value depended on their weight and purity. Every sale therefore required a scale, and buyers often cut bits from a larger piece to pay the exact amount. Sellers also had to worry that the metal had been mixed with cheaper materials.

More than 2,600 years ago, rulers in Lydia, a kingdom in what is now western Turkey, began producing small lumps of metal of a standard weight and stamping each one with an official image. The stamp acted as a guarantee: people no longer needed to weigh or test every piece, because the state stood behind its value.

The idea spread quickly to Greek cities, which created their own designs. Before long, coins were used not only in markets but also to pay soldiers and collect taxes, which made it far easier for governments to manage large economies.

screen.title: What Infants Expect
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant account of infant cognition held that babies younger than about eight months lack object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when they are out of sight. This conclusion rested largely on search tasks: when an attractive toy was covered by a cloth, young infants typically made no attempt to retrieve it.

Beginning in the 1980s, however, researchers adopted an alternative method that did not depend on reaching. Exploiting infants' tendency to look longer at surprising events, they presented apparently impossible scenes, such as a screen rotating straight through the space occupied by a hidden box. To warn neighbors about a planned interruption in service

why.es: Detalle (paráfrasis): la fecha pasó del lunes al miércoles, dos días más tarde. D inventa un motivo; el cambio se hizo porque los estudiantes pidieron más tiempo. A confunde el trabajo con la propia visita.

text: Residence Halls — New Recycling Rules

Beginning October 1, glass bottles and jars must go in the green bins in each building's basement instead of the blue bins on every floor. The blue bins will accept only paper, cans, and clean plastic containers. Pizza boxes and anything else with food on it belong in the regular trash. Halls that keep their bins correctly sorted all semester will be entered in a drawing for a free movie night.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To announce that the blue bins on each floor will be removed
To explain where residents should now put certain kinds of waste
To invite residents to help sort the recycling in the basement
To tell residents how they can sign up for a free movie night

why.en: Main purpose (paraphrase): the notice tells residents which bin to use for glass, for recyclables and for items with food on them. A is wrong because the blue bins stay; they simply accept fewer items. D turns a minor detail (the prize drawing) into the purpose.
why.tr: Ana amaç (parafraz): duyuru cam, geri dönüştürülebilir atıklar ve üzerinde yemek kalıntısı olan şeyler için hangi kutunun kullanılacağını anlatıyor. A yanlış, çünkü mavi kutular kaldırılmıyor; yalnızca daha az şey kabul ediyor. D küçük bir ayrıntıyı (ödül çekilişini) ana amaç sanıyor.
why.es: Propósito principal (paráfrasis): el aviso explica en qué contenedor va el vidrio, el material reciclable y lo que tiene restos de comida. A es incorrecta porque los contenedores azules se quedan; solo aceptan menos cosas. D convierte un detalle menor (el sorteo) en el propósito.

questions.stem: A resident has an empty yogurt container with some yogurt still inside. Where should it go?
options: Into one of the blue bins on that floor
Into a green bin in the basement
Next to the bins, for staff to sort later
In the regular trash

why.en: Application of a detail: the blue bins take only clean plastic, and anything with food on it belongs in the regular trash. A is the trap: the container is plastic, but it is not clean. B is only for glass bottles and jars.
why.tr: Ayrıntının uygulanması: mavi kutular yalnızca temiz plastik kabul ediyor; üzerinde yemek olan her şey normal çöpe gidiyor. A tuzak: kap plastik ama temiz değil. B yalnızca cam şişe ve kavanozlar için.
why.es: Aplicación de un detalle: los contenedores azules solo aceptan plástico limpio, y todo lo que tenga comida va a la basura normal. A es la trampa: el envase es de plástico, pero no está limpio. B es solo para botellas y frascos de vidrio.

text: Fine Arts Studios — Revised After-Hours Access

Beginning next semester, students who wish to use the ceramics and printmaking studios after 6 p.m. must complete a one-hour safety session before their ID cards will be activated for evening entry. Sessions are held every Tuesday during the first four weeks of the term; students who completed the session last year need not repeat it. Only studio staff may load the kilns, and their shifts end at 8 p.m., so pieces to be fired should be placed on the labeled shelf before then. No one may work in the studios alone after 10 p.m. Daytime access remains unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the main change described in the notice?
options: The ceramics and printmaking studios will close to everyone at 6 p.m.
Students will need a new kind of ID card to enter the studios by day
Studio staff will now stay until 10 p.m. to help students with the kilns
Night-time access to two studios will depend on prior instruction

why.en: Main change (paraphrase): after 6 p.m. the two studios can be used only after a safety session. A is too extreme; the studios stay open in the evening for trained students. C contradicts the notice, since staff shifts end at 8 p.m.
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz): saat 18.00'den sonra iki atölye ancak güvenlik eğitiminden sonra kullanılabilecek. A aşırı; atölyeler eğitim almış öğrencilere akşam da açık. C duyuruyla çelişiyor, çünkü personelin mesaisi saat 20.00'de bitiyor.

A es demasiado extremo; los talleres siguen abiertos por la noche para quien tenga la formación. C contradice el aviso, porque el turno del personal termina a las 8 p. m.

questions.stem: A student wants a vase fired in a kiln. What should she do?
options: Leave the vase on the marked shelf before 8 p.m.
Load the kiln herself after the Tuesday session
Bring the vase to the studio after 10 p.m. with a friend
Ask a staff member to open the kiln room at 9 p.m.

why.en: Application: only staff may load the kilns, and they leave at 8 p.m., so the piece must be on the labeled shelf before then. B is the trap: the safety session does not allow students to load kilns. D asks for staff at an hour when they have already gone.
why.tr: Uygulama: fırınlara yalnızca personel yükleme yapabilir ve personel saat 20.00'de çıkıyor; bu yüzden eser ondan önce etiketli rafa konmalı. B tuzak: güvenlik eğitimi öğrencilere fırın yükleme izni vermiyor. D personelin çoktan gitmiş olduğu bir saatte yardım istiyor.
why.es: Aplicación: solo el personal puede cargar los hornos y se va a las 8 p. m., así que la pieza debe estar en el estante etiquetado antes de esa hora. B es la trampa: la sesión de seguridad no permite a los estudiantes cargar los hornos. D pide ayuda al personal a una hora en la que ya se ha ido.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a student who attended the safety session last year?
options: She must attend another Tuesday session at the start of next term
She may stay in the studios alone at any hour of the night
She can get evening access without taking the session again
She is now permitted to load the kilns herself after 8 p.m.

why.en: Inference: students who "completed the session last year need not repeat it", so their cards can be activated without a new session. A contradicts this. B ignores the rule that no one may work alone after 10 p.m.
why.tr: Çıkarım: "completed the session last year need not repeat it" deniyor; yani bu öğrencinin kartı yeni bir eğitim almadan akşam girişine açılabilir. A bununla çelişiyor. B, saat 22.00'den sonra kimsenin yalnız çalışamayacağı kuralını yok sayıyor.
why.es: Inferencia: quienes "completed the session last year need not repeat it", así que su tarjeta se puede activar sin una nueva sesión. A contradice esto. B ignora la norma de que nadie puede trabajar solo después de las 10 p. m.
